seoTitle: What Conditions Qualify for Disability in Michigan? The 14 Listings, Explained
seoDescription: Which medical conditions qualify for Social Security disability in Michigan: SSA’s 14 body-system Listings with the actual criteria, how a condition that is not listed still qualifies through RFC and the grid rules, the mental-health B criteria, and what records prove each.
h1: Conditions That Qualify for Disability in Michigan
tagline: There is no list of conditions that qualify. There is a list of criteria, and a second path for everyone who does not meet them.
primaryKeyword: conditions that qualify for disability michigan
secondaryKeywords: what medical conditions qualify for social security disability
what qualifies for disability in michigan

c.v: Every week people in Michigan search for the list of conditions that qualify for Social Security disability, and every week they find pages that give them one. Those pages are not wrong, exactly, but they answer a question Social Security does not ask. No diagnosis qualifies anyone for disability benefits. What qualifies is a medically determinable impairment that has lasted or will last at least twelve months and either
meets or equals one of Social Security’s Listings of Impairments
or
leaves the person unable to do any work that exists in significant numbers
, given their age, education, and work history. The first path is the one the lists describe. The second path is the one most claimants are approved on.

This page covers both. It sets out the fourteen body systems of the Listings, the “Blue Book,” with the actual criteria for the listings Michigan claimants most often ask about, so that you can compare them to your own records. It explains the difference between meeting a listing and equaling one. Then it explains the path for everyone whose condition is severe but does not fit a listing: residual functional capacity, the grid rules that favor claimants over 50, and the medical-vocational allowance that accounts for a large share of approvals. It closes with what records prove each kind of claim.

Among the 7.2 million disabled workers receiving SSDI in December 2024, about a third were approved for musculoskeletal conditions and more than a quarter for mental disorders. Most of them did not meet a listing. They were approved because the evidence showed they could not work.

sections.heading: Path one: the Listings of Impairments

c.v: The Listings describe, for each body system, impairments severe enough that Social Security presumes a person who meets them cannot work. A listing has specific medical criteria, and
a claimant meets it only if the records document every element

. The table below gives the body systems with representative listings and a plain summary of what each requires. It is a guide to the records you need, not a substitute for the listing text at ssa.gov/disability/professionals/bluebook.
each summary against the current listing text before publication

head.v: What the records generally must show

rows.v: 1.15 spine disorders compromising a nerve root; 1.16 lumbar spinal stenosis; 1.18 major joint abnormality; 1.20 amputation; 1.21 soft tissue injury or abnormality under continuing surgical management

Imaging and examination findings, plus the specific functional limitations required by the applicable listing, which may include a documented medical need for a walker, bilateral canes or crutches, or a wheeled and seated mobility device; substantial loss of upper-extremity function; or other criteria specific to an amputation, fracture, or condition under continuing surgical management, lasting or expected to last 12 months.
2.02 loss of central visual acuity; 2.03 contraction of visual field; 2.10 hearing loss without cochlear implant; 2.11 with implant

Best-corrected acuity of 20/200 or less in the better eye; visual field testing; audiometry showing an average threshold of 90 dB (air) or word recognition of 40 percent or less; after cochlear implantation, disability is considered for one year following the initial implant, or the applicable post-implant HINT word-recognition score is 60 percent or less
3.02 chronic respiratory disorders (COPD, pulmonary fibrosis); 3.03 asthma; 3.04 cystic fibrosis; 3.09 pulmonary hypertension; 3.11 lung transplant

Condition-specific spirometry, DLCO, oxygenation testing, or qualifying hospitalizations, depending on the listing; for example, certain asthma claims require repeated qualifying hospitalizations. A lung transplant qualifies under listing 3.11 for three years.
4.02 chronic heart failure; 4.04 ischemic heart disease; 4.05 recurrent arrhythmias; 4.09 heart transplant; 4.12 peripheral arterial disease

Heart failure: imaging showing an ejection fraction of 30 percent or less or specified enlargement, plus persistent symptoms or three episodes of decompensation in 12 months or an abnormal exercise test; ischemic disease: specified stress test or angiographic findings; a transplant meets for one year
5.02 gastrointestinal hemorrhage requiring transfusion; 5.05 chronic liver disease; 5.06 inflammatory bowel disease; 5.08 weight loss from a digestive disorder; 5.09 liver transplant

Transfusions on specified occasions; chronic liver disease with qualifying complications or laboratory findings; inflammatory bowel disease with qualifying obstruction or other specified complications; BMI below 17.50 on at least two evaluations at least 60 days apart within 12 consecutive months despite prescribed treatment; a liver transplant qualifies for one year.
6.03 chronic kidney disease with dialysis; 6.04 kidney transplant; 6.05 CKD with impaired function; 6.09 complications requiring hospitalization
Ongoing dialysis; a transplant meets for one year; laboratory values (eGFR, creatinine, albumin) with specified complications; three hospitalizations of 48 hours or more in 12 months
7.05 hemolytic anemias including sickle cell disease; 7.08 thrombosis and hemostasis disorders; 7.10 bone marrow failure; 7.17 stem cell transplant; 7.18 repeated complications
Sickle cell: pain crises requiring IV narcotics six times in 12 months at least 30 days apart, or three hospitalizations of 48 hours; transplant meets for 12 months
8.08 burns; 8.09 chronic skin conditions with extensive lesions

Chronic skin lesions or contractures causing pain or other physical limitations that persist despite adherence to prescribed treatment for three months, together with the functional limitations required by the listing.
No separate listings since 2011; diabetes, thyroid, and adrenal disorders are evaluated under the body system they affect
Diabetic neuropathy under 11.14; retinopathy under 2.00; kidney disease under 6.00; recurrent hospitalizations for hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia under the affected system
Medical documentation establishing non-mosaic Down syndrome, such as qualifying karyotype evidence or a physician’s report meeting SSA’s specific diagnostic and descriptive requirements.
11.02 epilepsy; 11.04 stroke; 11.06 Parkinsonian syndrome; 11.09 multiple sclerosis; 11.10 ALS; 11.14 peripheral neuropathy; 11.18 traumatic brain injury

Epilepsy: generalized tonic-clonic seizures at least once a month for three months despite treatment, or dyscognitive seizures once a week for three months; stroke and TBI evaluated at least three months after the event for disorganization of motor function in two extremities or marked limitation in one area of functioning; ALS meets on diagnosis
12.02 neurocognitive; 12.03 schizophrenia; 12.04 depressive and bipolar; 12.05 intellectual disorder; 12.06 anxiety and OCD; 12.08 personality; 12.10 autism; 12.15 trauma and stressor-related (PTSD)
Medical documentation and the applicable functional criteria: generally paragraph B, with paragraph C available for certain listings; intellectual disorder under 12.05 has separate requirements.
13.02 head and neck; 13.10 breast; 13.13 nervous system; 13.14 lung; 13.20 pancreas; 13.23 female genital tract; 13.29 melanoma

Many cancers meet only when metastatic, recurrent, or inoperable; some meet on diagnosis (small cell lung cancer, pancreatic carcinoma other than islet cell, glioblastoma); For listings without a different specified period, listing-level disability generally continues until the cancer has been in complete remission for at least three years; SSA then evaluates any remaining impairments.
14.02 systemic lupus; 14.04 systemic sclerosis; 14.05 polymyositis; 14.06 undifferentiated connective tissue disease; 14.09 inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic); 14.11 HIV

Lupus: qualifying involvement of two or more organs or body systems, with at least moderate involvement of one and the required constitutional symptoms, or repeated manifestations with qualifying constitutional symptoms and marked functional limitation. inflammatory arthritis: persistent inflammation or deformity with inability to ambulate effectively or perform fine and gross movements, or involvement of two or more organ systems

c.v: Three things to take from the table. First, the listings are written in medical measurements, not symptoms: an ejection fraction, a spirometry value, a seizure frequency, a BMI. The records must contain the measurement. Second, several listings are met on diagnosis alone (ALS, non-mosaic Down syndrome, pancreatic cancer, small cell lung cancer), and most of those conditions are also on the Compassionate Allowances list for expedited handling; our
Compassionate Allowances page

covers that program. Third, the 2021 musculoskeletal revision and the 2017 mental revision made the two largest categories harder to meet, which is why the second path matters more than it did a decade ago.
The mental disorder listings: the B and C criteria
Mental health claims are the second-largest category and the most misunderstood. Nearly every mental listing from 12.02 through 12.15 requires two things:
medical documentation
of the disorder (the A criteria), and either the
B criteria
or the
C criteria
The
B criteria
measure functioning in four areas:
The claimant must have an
extreme limitation in one area or a marked limitation in two

. Social Security uses a five-point scale (none, mild, moderate, marked, extreme), and “marked” means seriously limited, “extreme” means unable to function in that area independently, appropriately, and effectively on a sustained basis. A diagnosis of major depression or PTSD with a treating psychiatrist’s records showing moderate limitations across the board does not meet the listing; the same diagnosis with documented marked limitations in concentration and in adapting, supported by treatment notes, hospitalizations, and a detailed psychiatric opinion, does.
The
C criteria

are the alternative for a “serious and persistent” disorder: a medically documented history of the disorder over at least two years, with ongoing treatment or a highly structured setting that diminishes the symptoms, and only marginal adjustment, meaning minimal capacity to adapt to changes or demands not already part of daily life. The C criteria exist for the claimant who is stable only because of intensive support and would decompensate at work.
Meeting versus equaling a listing
A claimant
meets
a listing when the records document every criterion. A claimant
equals

a listing, under 20 CFR 404.1526 and SSR 17-2p, when the impairment is at least equal in severity and duration to a listed one but does not match the criteria exactly: a listed impairment missing one finding but with other findings of equal significance, an unlisted impairment that is medically equivalent to a listed one, or a combination of impairments that together equal a listing. Equivalence requires a medical judgment by a Social Security medical consultant or a medical expert at the hearing; it is not something a claimant or a treating physician can declare. In practice, equivalence is argued at the hearing level and is most successful with a detailed opinion from a specialist explaining which listing and why.

sections.heading: Path two: residual functional capacity and the grid rules

c.v: Most people who receive disability benefits did not meet or equal a listing. They were approved at step five, because Social Security concluded, from their
residual functional capacity

and their vocational profile, that there was no work they could do. This is the medical-vocational allowance, and it is the path for the claimant with degenerative disc disease and a walker she does not quite need, the claimant with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 35 percent, the claimant with depression and anxiety whose limitations are marked in one area but moderate in the others.
Residual functional capacity

is what you can still do in a work setting on a regular and continuing basis, eight hours a day, five days a week, under 20 CFR 404.1545. Physically, it is expressed as an exertional level: sedentary (lifting 10 pounds occasionally, mostly sitting), light (20 pounds occasionally, 10 frequently, standing and walking about six hours), medium (50 pounds occasionally), heavy, or very heavy, together with non-exertional limits such as postural restrictions, reaching, handling, environmental restrictions, and the need to alternate positions or lie down. Mentally, it is expressed as the capacity for simple or detailed tasks, pace, attendance, interaction with the public and coworkers, and tolerance of change and stress.
The grid rules
, formally the Medical-Vocational Guidelines at 20 CFR Part 404, Subpart P, Appendix 2, take the exertional RFC and three vocational factors, age, education, and prior work, and direct a result:

head.v: How the grids treat a claimant limited to sedentary work

rows.v: Generally not disabled unless additional non-exertional limits erode the job base (illiteracy or inability to communicate in English is a factor at 45–49 for sedentary)

c.v: Disabled

rows.v: if no past relevant work or unskilled past work, or skilled work without transferable skills

c.v: Disabled

rows.v: unless skills transfer with very little adjustment

c.v: Disabled

rows.v: if unskilled past work or no transferable skills
Disabled unless skills transfer with very little adjustment

c.v: Two consequences follow. A 52-year-old warehouse worker with a bad back who can no longer lift 20 pounds and has no skills that transfer to a desk job is disabled under the grids even though his MRI does not meet listing 1.15. And a 38-year-old with the same back and the same RFC is not, unless non-exertional limitations (the need to lie down, absences, pain-related loss of concentration) are documented and eliminate the sedentary jobs the vocational expert would otherwise name. Social Security considers the age categories applicable during the period being evaluated. In a borderline situation within a few days to a few months of an older category, SSA considers whether to apply that older category rather than applying age mechanically, under 20 CFR 404.1563(b).).

For a claimant with mental limitations or a mix of physical and mental limitations, the grids are a framework rather than a directive, and the case is decided by the vocational expert’s testimony about whether jobs exist for a person with the specific limitations in the judge’s hypothetical. Our
appeals page
explains how that testimony is tested.

sections.heading: What the records have to show, for each path

c.v: To meet a listing

: the specific measurement or finding each criterion names, from the specialist who makes it: the echocardiogram report with the ejection fraction, the pulmonary function test with the FEV1, the seizure log and neurologist’s notes, the psychiatric treatment records and a mental RFC opinion addressing the four B areas, the pathology report with staging. A physician’s letter that says the patient “meets listing 4.02” without the underlying test is not evidence; the test is.
To win at step five
: a longitudinal treatment record without unexplained gaps; objective findings that correspond to the limitations claimed; and a
function-by-function opinion

from a treating source stating, in an eight-hour workday, how long the claimant can sit, stand, and walk, how much and how often they can lift, whether they need to change position or lie down, how often they would be off task and absent, and, for mental impairments, their capacity in each of the four B areas. Since 2017, under 20 CFR 404.1520c, that opinion is weighed for supportability and consistency rather than given controlling weight because it comes from a treating doctor, so the opinion must explain itself and match the records.
For both

: consistency between what you tell your doctors, what you write in Social Security’s Function Report, and what you say at the hearing, and evidence submitted at least five business days before the hearing under 20 CFR 404.935. Our
how to win your disability claim
page covers the evidence in detail, and our
how to apply
page covers getting it into the file from the start.

faqs.question: Is there a list of conditions that automatically qualify for disability?

answer.v: Not in the sense most people mean. A small number of listings are met on diagnosis (ALS, non-mosaic Down syndrome, pancreatic cancer, small cell lung cancer, among others), and the Compassionate Allowances program expedites claims for 314 serious conditions. For every other condition, qualification depends on documented severity and functional limitations, not the diagnosis.

faqs.question: My condition is not in the Blue Book. Can I still qualify?

answer.v: Yes, and most people who receive benefits did not meet a listing. If your condition is severe, has lasted twelve months, and the evidence shows you cannot do your past work or any other work given your age, education, and experience, you are disabled under the law.

Since the 2021 revision, the musculoskeletal listings require a documented need for a walker, two canes, or a wheelchair, or serious loss of use of the arms, so most back claims are decided at step five. Whether you qualify depends on your RFC and, heavily, on your age: a claimant over 50 limited to sedentary work with no transferable skills is disabled under the grid rules.

faqs.question: I have depression and anxiety. What do I have to prove?

answer.v: Medical documentation of the disorder, and either an extreme limitation in one of the four B areas or a marked limitation in two, or the C criteria for a serious and persistent disorder. Short of that, the claim is decided at step five on your mental RFC: your capacity for simple tasks, pace, attendance, and dealing with people and change.

faqs.question: Why does my age matter so much?

answer.v: Because the grid rules presume that a person over 50 limited to sedentary work, or over 55 limited to light work, without transferable skills, cannot adjust to other work. The same medical findings produce a different legal result at 49 and at 50.
An approval at step five, based on residual functional capacity and the vocational factors rather than on a listing. It is the most common basis for approval.

faqs.question: Can several conditions together qualify when none does alone?

answer.v: Yes. Social Security must consider the combined effect of all impairments, under 20 CFR 404.1523, both in determining whether they equal a listing and in assessing RFC.

faqs.question: I was approved for cancer. Will I lose benefits when treatment ends?

answer.v: A cancer that meets a listing is considered disabling for at least three years after treatment ends. After that, Social Security reevaluates the residual effects. Many claimants continue to qualify at step five on the lasting effects of treatment.

No. The Listings, the five-step test, and the grid rules are federal and apply identically in every state. What varies is the hearing office handling the case, its workload, and processing times. Michigan has seven SSA hearing offices, but federal disability eligibility standards remain the same.
